issues.explanation: 'Object Throwing' is a weak fit as a trauma trigger for a life-threatening accident; it implies a violence/conflict cue rather than an accident-linked reminder, and it does not connect well to the rest of the profile's vehicle/safety themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now
issues.explanation: 'Outsider' is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise accident-focused profile and lacks a clear clinical bridge to the selected triggers, threat items, or coping responses; it reads more like an interpersonal/identity aftermath than the central formulation presented here.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is questionable for a life-threatening accident unless the patient had a clear preventable role. As selected, the rest of the profile does not support a responsibility-based narrative strongly enough to make this appraisal cohere.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: 'Startle to Touch' is more suggestive of interpersonal assault-related threat than an accident-based threat pattern, and it is not well linked to the selected accident-relevant trigger/avoidance items.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Undereating is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The active formulation emphasizes a tight Triggers ↔ Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop centered on accident-related cues and danger responses, but food restriction does not plausibly function as a strategy for the stated triggers or threats and is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Startle to unexpected touch points more toward interpersonal assault-related threat sensitivity than the otherwise accident-focused pattern. With the listed triggers centered on vehicles, illness, and loss of autonomy, this item is not impossible but is notably weakly connected to the rest of the threat profile and trauma type.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: Guilt about not doing more to stop what happened is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening accident profile unless there is clear evidence of perceived preventability or responsibility. The rest of the appraisals emphasize helplessness and unfairness rather than responsibility, so this item pulls in a different direction and is hard to explain from the provided profile.

vignette: Six months ago, Claire's minivan hydroplaned off the county road during a sudden downpour. The steering wheel went slack in her hands, robbing her of any control, and the guardrail gave way with a sickening crunch. She felt nauseous and disoriented as the vehicle tumbled, her own body failing to brace or protect her. When the spinning stopped, she lay pinned against the door, coughing, watching other drivers swerve and collide in the chaos ahead. She filed reports about the road's poor drainage and the missing guardrail, but months of correspondence yielded nothing. She had come to believe what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. At first, crash imagery surfaced when she passed the county line, but it quickly bled into her daily rhythm. When she watched news footage of a pileup on the interstate, the image of her own crumpled hood and the shriek of tearing metal flooded her vision. Claire now scans for exits the moment she pushes through the heavy doors of the community center where she works in social ministry. Her eyes lock onto the fire door, the staff entrance, the stairwell, mapping every way out before she can even check her clipboard. She cannot trust safety, even when her supervisor assures her the building has passed inspection. The words feel hollow against the memory of metal shearing and glass shattering. Ordinary noises-a dropped stack of files, a chair scraping linoleum, a sudden ringtone-make her shoulders hike and her breath catch. She has come to believe she can no longer trust her own body. Around the same time, Claire found herself unable to drive. She refuses to be a passenger in any vehicle, too certain that surrendering the wheel means surrendering her life. She avoids situations that put her body under stress, such as climbing the three flights to the shelter office or lifting donation boxes. When her stomach turns or her knees weaken, she fears she will lose autonomy, forced to stop when she needs to keep moving. She also avoids relaxing because it feels dangerous. When she sits on her couch in the evenings, she keeps the television blaring, her muscles coiled, convinced that letting her guard down invites catastrophe. The patterns settled into her work without warning. In her role coordinating emergency relief for displaced families, she now sits in the corner of the supply room, refusing to move until she has verified every possible escape route. When volunteers press her to help load furniture into a van, the demand feels suffocating; she cannot stand the thought of being forced to do something while her body feels unwell. Across the weeks that followed, these responses did not fade. Instead, they stacked together, reshaping how she navigated both the community center and her own apartment. Her caseload thinned, her colleagues noticed the distance, and her single life, once filled with community outreach, narrowed. She has come to believe that injustice is the only constant, and that helplessness is the only reality. Today, Claire sits in the intake office, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her gaze tracking the two exits behind the therapist. She is here because the weight of scanning every doorway and bracing for every sound has left her exhausted. She is most afraid of collapsing in the middle of a street, of being forced into a situation her body cannot survive, but she is also quietly hoping that someone might finally help her believe that safety is possible to hold.
